title: A Compass for the Orchard
premise: In 1913, Dominic Marchetti drives for suffragist Edith Calloway, reading every letter she dictates before sealing it — a habit that keeps her safely outside history. When the seasonal bridge to the valley closes early, trapping the household with a dying orchard, a fugitive labor organizer hiding in the barn, and news that Edith's estranged daughter is coming home to claim her inheritance, Dominic's invisibility collapses. Forced to choose which of three desperate people gets the last berth on the supply wagon out before the river floods, she discovers that reading other people's words was always preparation for writing her own. She gives up the berth herself, testifies at an improvised hearing of the trapped household about the orchard owner's crimes, and ends the book crossing the rebuilt bridge in spring — no longer a driver, but the author of her own letters.
about_author: August Villalobos is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters in rural county collections. A Compass for the Orchard is their second novel, written in a farmhouse within sight of a river that floods every spring.

chapters.title: The Reader of Letters
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. She drives Edith through town, reads each dictated letter silently, and prides herself on being furniture. Establishes her philosophy: history happens to letter-writers, not drivers. Emotional beat: comfortable self-erasure, faintly cracked by one letter she almost doesn't seal.

chapters.title: Bridge Out
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The county posts notice: the bridge closes two months early for emergency repairs; the river is rising. Supplies must last until thaw. Edith refuses to leave. Beat: the first cold drop of confinement, disguised as logistics.

chapters.title: The Man in the Barn
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. While fetching apples she finds Tomás Reyes, a wounded organizer fleeing the mill owners' men, hiding among the crates. He begs her not to tell. Beat: fear braided with recognition — he read her face the way she reads letters.

chapters.title: What Edith Knows
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith has already found him and chosen silence, remembering her own years of hiding. She tests Dominic's loyalty without revealing why. Beat: two keepers of secrets circling each other politely.

chapters.title: The Daughter's Telegram
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A telegram arrives before the wires degrade: Edith's daughter Vivian will come for the estate — and the deed to the orchard, which legally includes the barn. If she arrives, Tomás is found. Beat: inheritance revealed as a weapon.

chapters.title: Rationing
chapters.summary: Cook Marta's POV. The household inventories food; Marta quietly feeds Tomás from her own portion. Dominic helps, crossing her first small line. Beat: solidarity as theft, warm and guilty.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Sorting Edith's correspondence, Dominic finds decades of unsent drafts — including one to Vivian, rewritten yearly, never mailed. Beat: grief; even the fearless have letters they can't deliver.

chapters.title: The Mill Men Ride Out
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. From the loft he watches searchers question neighbors at the far bank. He confesses to Dominic what he did: burned the mill's wage ledger to hide names. Beat: the price of survival made concrete — his safety costs others' wages.

chapters.title: Vivian at the Gate
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. She arrives by ferry before the crossing closes entirely, all sharp suits and sharper grievances, and immediately walks the property lines with a surveyor's eye. Beat: the intruder who is also family.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Vivian demands a full inventory; Dominic must list the barn's contents while concealing its occupant. She lies fluently for the first time and is shocked by how easily it comes. Beat: invisibility curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Floodwater Rising
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The river takes the low fields; the well turns brackish. The supply wagon company offers one final run — one berth — before the ford drowns for the season. Beat: the choice becomes real, with a deadline.

chapters.title: Three Names
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Three candidates emerge: Tomás, who will hang if caught; Marta's grandson, sick with fever across the river; and Edith, whose heart is failing. Dominic holds the deciding word because she holds the wagon contract. Beat: dread of arithmetic done on human lives.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Ghosts
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He reveals the burned ledger hid more than names — it proved the orchard's previous owner starved pickers through two winters, and Edith bought the land knowing. Beat: justice and inheritance shown as the same wound.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Parlor
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic confronts Edith with what Tomás told her. Edith neither denies nor apologizes: 'Survival is not a confession.' Beat: the mentor's fall; Dominic's faith cracks open.

chapters.title: Vivian Finds the Barn
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Following the survey map, Vivian discovers Tomás. Instead of raising alarm, she negotiates: his silence about her mother's past for hers about his presence. Beat: the antagonist revealed as another survivor making bargains.

chapters.title: The Fever Crossing
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic smuggles Marta's grandson onto the wagon under apple crates, giving up the berth she'd reserved for escape. The boy lives; the wagon sinks at the far bank; there will be no more crossings. Beat: sacrifice that closes doors behind it.

chapters.title: Edith's Collapse
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Edith's heart fails during the first frost. On her deathbed she asks Dominic to read her the unsent letter to Vivian aloud — then asks her to burn it. Beat: mercy versus truth; Dominic burns it and hates herself.

chapters.title: The Hearing in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating paragraphs. With the law unreachable across the flood, the trapped household convenes its own tribunal over the old owner's crimes and Tomás's arson. Dominic, keeper of everyone's words, is made to speak. Beat: justice outside the law, improvised and imperfect.

chapters.title: The Verdict
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The household rules Tomás's fire justified but binds him to stay and work the orchard through the thaw — punishment and refuge in one. Vivian, holding the deed now, must consent. She does, unexpectedly. Beat: grim, hard-won fairness.

chapters.title: What the River Takes
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Spring melt swells the river; Tomás saves Vivian from the collapsing boathouse, nearly drowning. Pulled out by Dominic, he understands he belongs to this place now. Beat: rescue as sentence and absolution together.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. At Edith's grave, Dominic finally writes a letter of her own — to the county, testifying to everything: the ledger, the hearing, the berth. She signs it and mails it before she can reconsider. Beat: the reader of letters becomes their author; terror and release.

chapters.title: Crossing Over
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The new bridge opens. Vivian stays to run the orchard with Tomás as foreman; Marta remains; Dominic boards the morning coach alone, carrying nothing but her own handwriting. Beat: quiet triumph — she chose no one's survival over her own, and survived anyway.
